summaries.example: Imagine a toy made from several pieces. Taurellus would say the pieces can work together without becoming one brand-new substance. In a similar way, he thought a human being is an arrangement of many basic forms, rather than one simple thing made from matter and form.
summaries.summary: Nicolaus Taurellus was an early modern philosopher who tried to explain nature while defending the Christian idea of creation. He rejected the view that everything is built from prime matter and form. Instead, he said that immaterial, form-like beings are the basic parts of reality. These forms can join together, but their joining usually makes only an accidental unity, like pieces working together rather than becoming one new substance. He therefore described human beings as collections of forms, a view that challenged familiar ideas about personhood. Taurellus also held that new forms and powers can arise when things interact, helping him explain plants, animals, and souls. He said God creates the world, but ordinary things have their own powers and do not need a new act of creation every moment. His ideas faced strong opposition, yet some parts of his metaphysics resemble ideas later associated with Leibniz.
key_ideas: Taurellus was a sixteenth-century philosopher who wanted philosophy and Christian theology to fit together.
He argued that the basic parts of nature are immaterial forms, not bits of prime matter.
He thought things can be joined together without becoming one single substance.
He explained new forms, including living forms, as arising from the activities and mixtures of other forms.
He argued that created things depend on God for their beginning but do not need God to keep remaking them every moment.
summaries.why_it_matters: Taurellus shows that people in the past asked deep questions about what makes something a real thing, how living beings begin, and how the world depends on God. His unusual answers also influenced later discussions about simple substances, activity, and the structure of reality. Studying him helps us see that scientific and philosophical ideas develop through arguments, disagreements, and attempts to connect different kinds of knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The study of what kinds of things exist and how they fit together.
A basic, form-like thing that can exist on its own rather than only inside something else.
The traditional idea of a basic material that receives a form. Taurellus rejected prime matter as a real part of created things.
A way something can be joined to other things without becoming one new substance.
A power to make a change happen or a power to be changed by something else.

questions_to_think_about: Can a group of parts be a real thing even if it is not one single substance?
What is the difference between making something and keeping it in existence?
If a new ability appears when things mix, where does that ability come from?
Why might people disagree with Taurellus’s account of human beings?

summaries.example: Consider a chemical mixture that develops a property not found in the ingredients taken separately. Taurellus uses a related philosophical idea: when forms interact, a new form can emerge with powers that are not merely a pile of the earlier powers. Yet he does not treat this new form as material or as made by combining smaller forms. It is simple because it is generated, although it can perish when the underlying conditions change.
summaries.summary: Nicolaus Taurellus was an early modern German philosopher who sought a unified philosophical and theological account of reality, especially one that could defend creation. His central move was to deny that prime matter is a genuine constituent of natural things. He retained form as the basic explanatory principle, but treated forms as immaterial entities with active and passive powers. Since a form need not inhere in a material subject, it can qualify as a substance in the sense of something capable of subsisting independently. Natural composites are therefore not substantial unities formed from matter and form; they are accidental conjunctions or aggregates of forms. This analysis extends to human beings and challenges traditional accounts of personhood. Taurellus also argues that mixtures can generate new, simple forms with powers not reducible to the powers of their ingredients. His treatment of plants, animals, and souls is thus compatible with an emergentist interpretation, though he discusses the theological question of human immortality separately. In debates with Cesalpino and with theories of Platonic emanation, Taurellus defends a plurality of substances and rejects the idea that the world is an accident of God or must be continuously produced by divine agency. The world depends on God for creation, but its forms and natural powers have their own subsistence.
key_ideas: Taurellus reworks Aristotelian form and matter by retaining forms while denying prime matter as a constituent of the natural world.
His criterion of substantiality is independent subsistence; because forms can subsist without prime matter, they can count as substances.
Composition is accidental rather than substantial: a complex being is an aggregate of forms, and the human being is not a substantial unity in the traditional sense.
He explains the hierarchy of forms through causal activity and receptivity: more noble forms act more, while less noble forms are more receptive.
His account of souls is partly naturalistic and emergentist. Mixtures can generate forms with powers exceeding the powers of their elements, while human soul and body are mutually related.

Against monism and emanation, he distinguishes creation dependence from continued subsistence dependence. Created things originate through God but possess their own powers and do not require continuous divine conservation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Taurellus is important because he occupies a revealing position between late scholastic philosophy and later early modern metaphysics. His immaterial forms, substance pluralism, account of causal powers, and defense of independent created substances anticipate themes often associated with Leibniz, who knew and admired his work. His case also illustrates how changing one assumption—whether prime matter is real—can reshape theories of composition, life, personhood, divine action, and the eternity of the world. The entry preserves these as historical arguments rather than presenting them as settled conclusions.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical investigation of being, reality, composition, dependence, and the kinds of entities that exist.
An entity that subsists in itself rather than existing only in another entity as an accident.

The Aristotelian material principle supposed to underlie forms. Taurellus denies that it is a constituent of natural beings and sometimes uses the term metaphorically for absolute non-being before creation.
A unity whose members are joined but do not constitute one substance by essence.
A relation in which one entity requires another in order to exist or persist.
The appearance of a new form or causal power through the interaction or mixture of prior forms, without reducing the new power to their mere sum.
A theory that one substance, such as God or a unique intellect, underlies all other beings or makes them merely its accidents.
A theory that created reality proceeds or flows from a divine source, often implying ongoing dependence on that source.

Can a human being be an aggregate rather than a substantial unity without losing personal identity?
How does Taurellus’s emergent account of souls differ from saying that souls are simply combinations of bodily powers?
Why does Taurellus think continuous emanation would threaten the stability of natural things?
Does defending creation require that created beings remain ontologically independent after they are created?

summaries.example: Think about a sports team. The players can cooperate and produce a result, but the team is not necessarily a new kind of person. Taurellus used a more serious version of this idea when discussing nature: several forms can be connected and work together without making one substantial thing. He applied this to human beings, saying that a person is an aggregate of forms rather than a single substantial unity. This was one reason his view seemed to challenge traditional ideas about what a person is.
summaries.summary: Nicolaus Taurellus was a philosopher of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. He worked in a period when scholars were debating Aristotle, theology, medicine, and the structure of nature. Taurellus hoped to give one account that respected both philosophy and Christian belief in creation. His most distinctive idea was that the basic constituents of reality are immaterial forms. He denied that prime matter is a real ingredient underneath those forms. Forms have powers: they can cause changes, and they can receive changes from other forms. When forms are joined, the result is usually an aggregate, not a new substance made from all of them. This led Taurellus to say that human beings lack substantial unity, a claim that challenged traditional accounts of personhood. He also argued that mixtures can produce new forms with new powers. This helped him explain the organization of plants and animals and the origin of souls in a natural way, although he still considered the theological question of immortality. Taurellus rejected substance-monist accounts that make the world or all minds parts of one substance. He also criticized emanation theories that make created things flow continuously from God. In his view, God creates the world, while natural forms have their own powers and can continue to exist without being recreated at every instant. His work was controversial but later appeared to anticipate some ideas connected with Leibniz.
key_ideas: Taurellus wanted philosophical reasoning and Christian teaching about creation to support one another.
He rejected the standard picture in which prime matter and form together make physical things.
For him, forms are the basic entities, and they have both powers to act and abilities to be affected.
A composition can be real and useful without being a single substance; he applied this claim to human beings.
He thought living forms could arise from mixtures and could have powers greater than those of the elements involved.
He opposed views saying that the whole world is one substance or that created things must be continuously produced by God.
summaries.why_it_matters: Taurellus matters because his arguments connect several questions that are often studied separately: what a substance is, how parts make wholes, how living beings arise, and how God relates to the world. His answers were controversial, but they show how a philosopher can revise an old theory while keeping some of its vocabulary. They also help explain why later historians notice similarities between Taurellus and Leibniz, even though Taurellus had his own system and purposes.

important_terms.definition: The study of reality: what exists, what things are made of, and how things depend on one another.
A thing that can exist in itself, rather than only as a feature of another thing.
A proposed basic material beneath all physical forms. Taurellus argued that it is not really part of created natural things.
A group of things that belong together but do not form one substance.
A way of existing in another thing, such as a feature or property that needs a substance to support it.
A new form or ability that appears when things interact and is not just the sum of what they had before.
The view that everything is ultimately one substance, with other things treated as parts, features, or expressions of it.

questions_to_think_about: Is a team, family, or school one thing, or only a collection of individuals?
Why might someone think that a property needs a substance to exist?
Could a new ability emerge from a mixture without being found in any ingredient alone?
Why would Taurellus’s view of human beings worry theologians?
What is the difference between being created by God and needing God to sustain every moment of existence?
